sheet.howExamined: M8, Paper 1 (no calculator) or Paper 2 (calculator), 50 marks in 75 minutes each; a probability question in almost every series from 2019 to 2026, usually in the second half. Four shapes recur. Two items taken without replacement, 4 marks for the same colour or one of each as one part: a mark for each product, one for adding and one for the answer (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q11, Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q13, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q14). Three colours: 3 marks for both of one colour, then 4 or 5 for different colours, most quickly 1 minus the same colour (November 2022 M8 Paper 2 Q13, November 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q12, Summer 2026 M8 Paper 1 Q12). A tree drawn or completed from sentences in which the second chance depends on the first, a mark for each pair of branches, then 2 for a probability read from it (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q8, November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q9, Summer 2026 M8 Paper 2 Q9). Group sizes with a probability for each, 4 marks, answered by counting first (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q7, November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q1, November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q3). The A* end puts a letter in the bag and asks for the equation (Summer 2021 M8 Paper 2 Q11, Summer 2022 M8 Paper 1 Q15). Most bag questions say only 'taken at random'; the second pick is still out of one fewer.
traps: Keeping the first-pick denominator on the second pick, so the item is in effect put back; on Summer 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q13, an A* same-colour question, over 70 per cent had full marks

Lowering the denominator but not the numerator when the same type was taken; Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q11, a non-replacement question the report called difficult, was answered impressively, a majority with full marks
Adding along a branch instead of multiplying (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q9)
Counting one order of a two-colour outcome instead of both (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q4; November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q14)
Multiplying the two branch results instead of adding them
Answering at least one with the probability of none, or with the probability of exactly one
Doing two trials when the question asks for three (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q9)
Arithmetic slips multiplying simple fractions by hand (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 1 Q11; November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q14)
Leaving labels off the branches, or writing counts where probabilities go (November 2025 M8 Paper 2 Q6; November 2024 M8 Paper 1 Q7; Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q8)
Using one branch, or three, where the description fits two (Summer 2023 M8 Paper 2 Q9)

Dividing by the whole group when the question chooses from part of it: count the ones who fit, then put that count on the bottom (Summer 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q7; November 2024 M8 Paper 2 Q1; November 2025 M8 Paper 1 Q3, where fewer than half had full marks)
Reading 'two are taken at random' as with replacement: unless the item is put back, the second pick is out of one fewer
Writing a probability as a ratio, or leaving an answer greater than 1 unchecked

noteBlocks.md: In the drawing, the first pick comes from all 11 counters. Whichever colour it is, that counter stays out, so every second-pick branch is over 10.
The top changes only for the colour that was taken. After a red, 3 of the 10 are red and all 7 blues are still there. After a blue, all 4 reds are there but only 6 blues.

noteBlocks.stem: A bag holds $4$ red and $7$ blue counters. Two are taken at random, and the first is not put back. Complete the tree diagram.

steps.decision: Count the whole bag: 11 counters, 4 of them red. The two branches from one point add to 1.
One red has gone, so 10 counters are left and only 3 are red. None of the blues has moved.
This time a blue has gone: still 10 left, all 4 reds, and 6 blues. Each pair adds to 1.

noteBlocks.task: Set up two picks without replacement and change the counts. Watch what the second-pick denominators do, and check each time that the four branch products still add to 1.

noteBlocks.prompt: A jar holds $5$ lemon and $9$ orange sweets. An orange one is taken and eaten. What is the probability that the next sweet taken is orange?
noteBlocks.explain: The second pick comes from a smaller jar: 13 sweets, because one was eaten, and 8 oranges, because the eaten one was orange. That is step 2 of See it with oranges for reds. Keeping 9 on top forgets the eaten orange; keeping 14 underneath puts it back.

twin.prompt: A tray holds $7$ plain and $6$ seeded rolls. A seeded roll is taken. What is the probability that the next roll taken is seeded?
twin.explain: One roll has gone, so 12 are left, and it was seeded, so 5 seeded rolls are left: 5/12. The top falls only for the kind that was taken.

optionNotes.why: The seeded roll that was taken is not on the tray any more, so the seeded count is one fewer.
That is the first pick's chance; the roll is not put back, so the second pick is out of one fewer.
The seeded count fell but the tray total did not; one roll has gone, so the bottom falls by one too.
Counting the oranges you started with is natural, but the one that was eaten is not there any more, so the top is one fewer.
That is the chance on the first pick; nothing goes back into the jar, so the second pick is out of one fewer sweet.
You took one off the oranges but left the jar at its old total; a sweet has gone, so the bottom falls by one as well.

noteBlocks.md: Along a branch, multiply: both picks have to happen. Across branches, add: two different branches are two different ways for one description to come true. 'The same colour' is two branches, red then red and blue then blue, so it is two products added.

noteBlocks.title: Why multiply along a branch
noteBlocks.md: $\tfrac{4}{11}$ of all pairs start with a red. Of those, 3 in every 10 go on to a second red. So red then red happens 3/10 of 4/11 of the time, and 'of' is multiply: $\tfrac{4}{11} \times \tfrac{3}{10}$.

noteBlocks.stem: From the bag of $4$ red and $7$ blue counters, two are taken at random without replacement. Work out the probability that both counters match in colour.

steps.decision: Along the red, red branch: multiply. The second fraction comes off the tree after a red.
The blue, blue branch in the same way.
Two branches fit 'the same colour', so add them. The denominators already match.
Divide top and bottom by 2. Schemes take either form; simplify when the question asks for the simplest form.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box holds $2$ gold and $7$ silver coins. Two are taken at random without replacement. Which calculation gives the probability that both match in colour?
noteBlocks.explain: 'The same colour' is two branches, gold then gold and silver then silver, as in steps 1 to 3 of See it: multiply along each branch, then add the two. Multiplying all four fractions joins the branches with the wrong operation; 9 underneath twice puts the first coin back; one product is one branch only.

twin.prompt: A drawer holds $2$ black and $6$ white socks. Two are taken at random without replacement. Which calculation gives the probability that both match in colour?
twin.explain: Two branches fit: black then black, and white then white. Multiply along each, with the second pick over one fewer, then add the two products.

optionNotes.why: The two branches are separate ways to get a matching pair, so their products are added, not multiplied together.
The first sock is not put back, so the second fraction is out of one fewer.
White then white is only one of the two matching branches; black then black counts too.
A times sign looks like 'and', but the two branches are two different ways to get matching colours, so their results add.
Keeping the full box underneath treats the first coin as put back; without replacement the second pick is out of one fewer.
Silver then silver is one way to match, but gold then gold is another, and both branches count.

noteBlocks.text: One of each: count both orders

noteBlocks.md: 'One of each colour' does not say which comes first, so red then blue and blue then red both fit. Their products use the same numbers in a different order, so they are equal, but write both: the scheme gives a mark for each product and one for adding them.

noteBlocks.stem: From the bag of $4$ red and $7$ blue counters, two are taken at random without replacement. Work out the probability that one is red and one is blue.

steps.decision: Red first, then blue: all 7 blues are still in the bag.
Blue first, then red: the same numbers in the other order, so the same product.
Both orders fit 'one of each', so add them.
Simplify. Check: with the same colour, 27/55 + 28/55 = 1, because every pair is one or the other.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two cards are taken at random without replacement from $3$ red and $7$ black cards. What is the probability of one red card and one black card?
noteBlocks.explain: Red then black and black then red both fit, as steps 1 to 3 of See it: 21/90 each way, so 42/90 = 7/15. Stopping at one order gives half of that; 10 under the second pick puts the first card back; red then red is a different branch.

twin.prompt: Two counters are taken at random without replacement from $2$ red and $9$ black. What is the probability of one of each colour?
twin.explain: Both orders fit: 18/110 for red then black, the same for black then red, so 36/110 = 18/55.

optionNotes.why: One order only gives half the answer; the other order is a separate branch with the same product.
Using the full bag twice puts the first counter back.
Red then red has no black counter in it, so it cannot be one of each.
Red then black is right, but black then red is a second branch with the same product, and it has to be added.
Squaring off the second pick at the full pack is what happens when the first card goes back, which it does not here.
Red then red is a branch where both cards match, so it is not one red and one black.

noteBlocks.caption: Nine colour pairs, three of them the same colour. Work out those three and take them from 1.

noteBlocks.md: With three colours, 'different colours' fits six branches but 'the same colour' fits only three. Every pair of picks is one or the other, so work out the same colour and take it from 1: three products to multiply by hand instead of six.

noteBlocks.stem: A box holds $4$ red, $3$ yellow and $2$ white pegs. Two are taken at random without replacement. Work out the probability that the two colours differ.

steps.decision: The same colour first: red then red, over 9 and then 8.
Yellow then yellow is 3/9 × 2/8; white then white is 2/9 × 1/8.
Add the three same-colour branches.
Every pair is the same colour or different, so take the same colour from 1.
Simplify: 52 and 72 share 4.

noteBlocks.prompt: Two counters are taken at random without replacement from $6$ green, $5$ yellow and $1$ white. What is the probability that the two colours differ?
noteBlocks.explain: Only green-green and yellow-yellow can happen, because there is one white: 50/132 in all. Every other pair differs, so 1 − 50/132 = 82/132 = 41/66, as steps 3 to 5 of See it did. 25/66 is the same colour itself; 41/132 counts one order of each pair; 41/72 puts the first counter back.

twin.prompt: Two beads are taken at random without replacement from $3$ red, $3$ blue and $4$ green. What is the probability that the two do not match in colour?
twin.explain: The same colour is 24/90: red-red, blue-blue and green-green added. Not the same colour is everything else, so 1 − 24/90 = 66/90 = 11/15.

optionNotes.why: That is the same colour itself; not the same colour is 1 minus it.
Every mixed pair has two orders, and one order of each is only half of them.
The full bag under the second pick puts the first bead back, which does not happen here.
That is the chance of the same colour; different colours is what is left when it is taken from 1.
Each mixed pair can happen in either order, so counting one order of each gives only half.
Keeping the full bag under the second pick puts the first counter back, which does not happen here.

noteBlocks.text: At least one: one minus none

noteBlocks.md: 'At least one red' fits every branch but one: the branch with no red at all, blue then blue. So work out that single branch and take it from 1. 'Neither is red' is that same branch, asked for directly.

noteBlocks.stem: From the bag of $4$ red and $7$ blue counters, two are taken at random without replacement. Work out the probability that at least one is red.

steps.decision: The only branch with no red: blue, then blue.
At least one red is every branch except that one.
Simplify. The long way agrees: red-red, red-blue and blue-red make 12 + 28 + 28 = 68 over 110.

noteBlocks.prompt: A bag holds $2$ green and $8$ white marbles. Two are taken at random without replacement. What is the probability that at least one is green?
noteBlocks.explain: The only branch with no green is white then white, 56/90; take it from 1 to get 34/90 = 17/45, as steps 1 and 2 of See it did. 28/45 is that no-green branch itself; 16/45 is exactly one green, which leaves out green-green.

twin.prompt: A bag holds $3$ red and $10$ blue counters. Two are taken at random without replacement. What is the probability that at least one is red?
twin.explain: No red is blue then blue, 90/156, so at least one red is 66/156 = 11/26.

optionNotes.why: That is the no-red branch itself, which has to be taken from 1.
Exactly one red misses the branch where both are red.
Both red is only one of three branches with a red in them.
That is the one branch with no green at all; at least one green is everything else, so it comes from 1 minus this.
Exactly one green leaves out the branch where both are green, which also has at least one.
Both green is only one of the branches that hold a green; the one-green branches count as well.

noteBlocks.stem: The probability that Ciara cycles to school is $0.8$; otherwise she takes the bus. If she cycles, the probability that she is on time is $0.95$. If she takes the bus, it is $0.6$. Work out the probability that she is late.

steps.decision: The first pair of branches adds to 1.
The 'if she cycles' sentence gives the on-time branch; late is what is left of 1.

steps.working: After the bus: on time $0.6$, late $0.4$
steps.decision: The bus has its own sentence, so its own pair of branches.
Late happens two ways: cycling then late, and the bus then late. Multiply along each.
Add the two ways.

noteBlocks.title: Conditional Probability - Corbettmaths
noteBlocks.why: Corbettmaths video 247, on probabilities that depend on what happened first. Watch it beside the steps above, then answer the check.

noteBlocks.prompt: The probability that it rains on Saturday is $0.4$. If it rains, the probability that the match is called off is $0.3$; if it does not rain, it is $0.05$. What is the probability that the match is called off?
noteBlocks.explain: Called off happens two ways, rain then off and no rain then off, as steps 4 and 5 of See it: 0.4 × 0.3 + 0.6 × 0.05 = 0.15. 0.12 is the rain branch alone; 0.35 adds the two 'if' chances without their first branches; 0.14 puts 0.4 on the no-rain branch.

twin.prompt: The probability that a day is windy is $0.25$. If it is windy, the probability that the ferry is cancelled is $0.4$; if not, it is $0.02$. What is the probability that the ferry is cancelled?
twin.explain: Two branches end in a cancellation: 0.25 × 0.4 + 0.75 × 0.02 = 0.115. The not-windy branch carries 0.75, not 0.25.

optionNotes.why: The ferry can also be cancelled on a calm day, so that branch is added to the windy one.
Adding the two 'if' chances skips the first branches they belong to.
The calm branch carries 1 minus the windy chance, not the windy chance again.
The rain branch is one way for the match to be called off, but it can also be called off when it stays dry, so that branch is added.
The two 'if' chances belong to different first branches, so each must be multiplied by its first branch before they are added.
The dry branch carries 1 minus the chance of rain, not the chance of rain again.

noteBlocks.stem: A club has $150$ members: $80$ adults and $70$ juniors. The probability that an adult swims is $\tfrac{1}{4}$, and for a junior it is $0.6$. A member who swims is chosen at random. Work out the probability that this member is a junior.

steps.decision: The expected number: the probability times the group size.
The same for the juniors.
The member is chosen from the swimmers only.
42 of the 62 swimmers are juniors. Dividing by 150 would answer a different question.

noteBlocks.prompt: Year 11 has $140$ pupils: $60$ girls and $80$ boys. The probability that a girl walks to school is $0.4$, and for a boy it is $\tfrac{3}{8}$. One of the walkers is picked at random. How likely is it that the walker is a boy?
noteBlocks.explain: Count first, as steps 1 to 3 of See it: 24 girls and 30 boys walk, 54 walkers in all, so 30 out of 54 is 5/9. 3/14 divides by every pupil; 3/8 is the boys' own chance; 4/9 is the girls' share of the walkers.

twin.prompt: A car park holds $200$ cars: $120$ petrol and $80$ electric. The probability that a petrol car is blue is $0.25$, and for an electric car it is $0.5$. A blue car is chosen at random. What is the probability that it is electric?
twin.explain: 30 petrol and 40 electric cars are blue, 70 blue cars in all, so 40 out of 70 is 4/7.

optionNotes.why: The car is chosen from the blue cars, so the blue cars go on the bottom, not every car.
That is the chance that an electric car is blue, not the chance that a blue car is electric.
That is the petrol cars' share of the blue cars, the other group.
Dividing by every pupil answers a different question, because the pupil is chosen only from those who walk.
That is the chance that a boy walks, not the chance that a walker is a boy.
That is the girls' share of the walkers, the other group.

noteBlocks.md: **'Two are taken at random.'** Of the eight questions from November 2022 to Summer 2026 that take two items from a bag or a box, six never say 'without replacement'. You cannot take the same item twice, so the second pick is out of one fewer.
**Three picks.** A third pick is a third factor. Summer 2024 Paper 1 Q9 repeated a pick three times and some answers used only two factors. Without replacement the bottom falls each time.
**'Show that'.** When the answer is printed (Summer 2023 Paper 1 Q11), every mark is in the working: write each product and the sum before the given fraction.

noteBlocks.stem: A bowl holds $6$ green and $2$ red apples. Three are taken at random. Show that the probability that all three are green is $\tfrac{5}{14}$.

steps.decision: 'Taken at random' means none goes back: three picks, three factors, the bottoms falling 8, 7, 6.
Multiply the tops and the bottoms.
Divide top and bottom by 24 to reach the printed answer. In a show that, this line earns its mark only with the lines above it.

noteBlocks.prompt: A question says: three counters are taken at random from $4$ red and $9$ blue; work out the probability that all three are red. What is the first line?
noteBlocks.explain: At random means nothing goes back, and three picks means three factors, as in step 1 of See it: 13 counters, then 12, then 11, with one fewer red each time. Two factors stop a pick short; 4/13 three times puts each counter back; adding joins the picks with the wrong operation.

twin.prompt: Three crisp packets are taken at random from $10$ plain and $4$ salted. What is the first line for the probability that all three are plain?
twin.explain: Three picks, none put back: three factors, with the tops falling 10, 9, 8 and the bottoms 14, 13, 12.

optionNotes.why: Three packets are taken, so there are three factors, not two.
The same fraction three times puts each packet back, which does not happen.
All three picks must happen, so the fractions multiply.
Two factors stop one pick short; three counters are taken, so there are three factors.
Using the full bag three times puts each counter back, but at random nothing goes back.
The three picks all have to happen, one after another, so the fractions multiply rather than add.

noteBlocks.text: Going further: a letter in the bag

noteBlocks.md: The hardest version hides a number. The bag holds $n$ counters, 3 of them red, and the probability of two reds is given. The tree works as always, with $n$ in place of a count, and the equation it gives is a quadratic.

noteBlocks.title: Where the specification stops
noteBlocks.md: Notation such as P(A | B), Bayes' theorem, trees read backwards and trees with more than three stages are beyond this specification.

noteBlocks.stem: A bag holds $n$ counters, $3$ of which are red. Two are taken at random without replacement. The probability that both are red is $\tfrac{1}{15}$. Show that $n^2 - n - 90 = 0$, and find $n$.

steps.decision: Red then red: 3 of $n$, then 2 of the $n - 1$ left.
Cross-multiply: 6 over $n(n - 1)$ equals 1 over 15.
Expand the bracket and gather everything on one side: the equation asked for.
A number of counters cannot be negative, so $n = -9$ is rejected.

noteBlocks.prompt: A box holds $x$ buttons, $2$ of them black. Two are taken at random without replacement, and the probability that both are black is $\tfrac{1}{21}$. How many buttons are in the box?
noteBlocks.explain: Both black is 2/x × 1/(x − 1), as in step 1 of See it, so 2 over x(x − 1) is 1/21 and x(x − 1) = 42. Two whole numbers one apart multiply to 42: 7 × 6. A count cannot be negative, so x = 7.

twin.prompt: A bag holds $n$ counters, $2$ of them red. Two are taken at random without replacement, and the probability that both are red is $\tfrac{1}{28}$. How many counters are in the bag?

noteBlocks.md:
Write each second-pick probability over one fewer, with one fewer on top for the colour taken.
Multiply along a branch, and add every branch that fits, both orders included.
Take the same colour from 1 for different colours, and none from 1 for at least one.
Read 'if' sentences into their own branches, and count groups before choosing from them.

Expect one question most series, on either paper, worth 4 to 7 marks: a same-colour or one-of-each question as one 4-mark part, three colours for 4 or 5 more, or a tree to complete, a mark for each pair of branches, and then read. The first marks are the products along the branches, the last is the sum. Stuck: draw the tree and label every branch, because the pairs score on their own.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability of no toffee at all. Everything else has at least one, so subtract it from 1: $1 - \tfrac{14}{39} = \tfrac{25}{39}$.
That is exactly one toffee. At least one also allows two toffees, so that branch belongs in the total as well.

Two are taken at random, without replacement.

Work out the probability that both are dark.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: After one dark chocolate, $3$ dark are left out of $9$.
Cancel before multiplying to keep the numbers small.

commonErrors.feedback: Both fractions are $\tfrac{4}{10}$, so the first chocolate went back into the box. The second denominator is $9$ and the second numerator is $3$.
Adding the counts and the totals collapses the two picks into one fraction. Each pick is its own probability, and they multiply.

parts.stem:
Three chocolates are now taken at random from the box of $4$ dark and $6$ milk, without replacement.

Work out the probability that all three are dark.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Three picks means three fractions.
Each denominator falls by one, and so does each numerator.

commonErrors.feedback: Every denominator stayed at $10$, so each chocolate went back. Without replacement they fall to $9$ and then $8$.
That is two dark chocolates, not three. A third trial means a third factor.

parts.stem:
The tree diagram is for two counters taken at random, without replacement, from $7$ blue and $5$ yellow counters.

Write down the probability that belongs in the empty box: yellow on the second pick, after a blue on the first.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: A blue counter has been removed.
Does the number of yellows change?
parts.workedSolution: A blue counter was taken, so all $5$ yellows are still in the bag but the total has fallen to $11$: the probability is $\tfrac{5}{11}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the first-pick probability of yellow. One counter has already gone, so the denominator is $11$.
A blue counter was taken, not a yellow one, so all $5$ yellows are still there. Only the total has fallen.

context.setting: A jar of beads, two taken at random one after the other

parts.stem:
Niamh has a jar holding $6$ red beads and $5$ green beads.

She takes a bead at random and does not put it back. She then takes a second bead at random.

Work out the probability that her two beads are the same colour.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Same colour means both red or both green.
Work out each one, then add them.
The second denominator is one less than the first.
parts.workedSolution: Both red: $\tfrac{6}{11} \times \tfrac{5}{10} = \tfrac{30}{110}$. Both green: $\tfrac{5}{11} \times \tfrac{4}{10} = \tfrac{20}{110}$. Adding: $\tfrac{30}{110} + \tfrac{20}{110} = \tfrac{50}{110}$, which is $\tfrac{5}{11}$.

commonErrors.feedback: Both denominators stayed at $11$, so the bead was replaced. Each second-pick denominator is $10$, and the numerator falls too because the same colour was taken.
That is both red only. Both green is a second way of being the same colour, and it has to be added on.
The two branches were multiplied. Either branch will do, so they are added instead.

parts.stem:
A box holds $9$ batteries. $3$ of them are flat and the rest are good.

Two batteries are taken from the box at random, without replacement.

Complete the tree diagram.

rubric: First pair of branches labelled flat and good, with 3/9 and 6/9
Second branches after a flat: 2/8 and 6/8
Second branches after a good one: 3/8 and 5/8
Every branch carries both a label and a probability, and each pair sums to 1

hints: The first denominators are $9$.
Every second denominator is $8$.
Each pair of branches must add to 1.
parts.workedSolution: First pick: $P(\text{flat}) = \tfrac{3}{9}$, $P(\text{good}) = \tfrac{6}{9}$. After a flat battery: $\tfrac{2}{8}$ flat and $\tfrac{6}{8}$ good. After a good one: $\tfrac{3}{8}$ flat and $\tfrac{5}{8}$ good. Each pair adds to 1.

commonErrors.feedback: Every branch needs a label and a probability. A tree with the numbers missing cannot earn the marks that follow from it.

parts.stem:
Work out the probability that exactly one of the two batteries is flat.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: both orders used: 18/72 and 18/72, from their tree

hints: Exactly one flat can happen two ways.
Multiply along each branch, then add.
parts.workedSolution: Flat then good is $\tfrac{3}{9} \times \tfrac{6}{8} = \tfrac{18}{72}$, and good then flat is $\tfrac{6}{9} \times \tfrac{3}{8} = \tfrac{18}{72}$. Adding gives $\tfrac{36}{72} = \tfrac{1}{2}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is flat first, working second. The other order counts too, so both products are added.
Along a branch both things happen, so the two probabilities multiply. Adding them gives a number far too large.

parts.stem:
Work out the probability that at least one of the two batteries is flat.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: 1 - 30/72, or the three matching branches added

hints: The only outcome with no flat battery is good then good.
Subtract that from 1.
parts.workedSolution: $P(\text{neither flat})$ is $\tfrac{6}{9} \times \tfrac{5}{8} = \tfrac{30}{72}$, which is $\tfrac{5}{12}$, so $P(\text{at least one flat}) = 1 - \tfrac{5}{12} = \tfrac{7}{12}$. The long route gives $6 + 18 + 18 = 42$ over $72$, the same fraction.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability that neither battery is flat. Subtract it from 1: $1 - \tfrac{5}{12} = \tfrac{7}{12}$.
That is exactly one flat battery, which is part (b). At least one also includes both being flat.

questions.solutionProgram: tree for 3 flat of 9; exactly one = 18/72 + 18/72 = 1/2; at least one = 1 - 30/72 = 7/12

context.setting: A tin of three kinds of biscuit, two taken at random

parts.stem:
A tin holds $3$ plain biscuits, $4$ chocolate biscuits and $5$ ginger biscuits.

Two biscuits are taken from the tin at random.

Work out the probability that both biscuits are ginger.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Two taken at random: the second is out of one fewer.
Both ginger is one branch: multiply along it.

commonErrors.feedback: That keeps 12 under the second pick, as if the first biscuit went back. Two taken at random leaves 11, with 4 of them ginger.
Both biscuits have to be ginger, one after the other: multiply along the branch, do not add.
The bottom fell to 11, but the top must fall too: one ginger has gone, so 4 are left.

parts.stem: Work out the probability that the two biscuits are different types.

scheme.for: 38/132 seen as the same-type total, or 94/132

hints: Different types fits six branches; the same type fits three.
Work out the same type and take it from 1.
parts.workedSolution: Same type: $\tfrac{6}{132} + \tfrac{12}{132} + \tfrac{20}{132}$, which is $\tfrac{38}{132}$. Different types: $1 - \tfrac{38}{132} = \tfrac{94}{132}$, which is $\tfrac{47}{66}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability of two of the same type. Different types is what is left when it is taken from 1.
Each mixed pair can come in either order, so each product counts twice. The quicker route is 1 minus the same type.
That keeps 12 under the second pick, as if the first biscuit went back.

context.setting: A bag of red, blue and one white counter

parts.stem:
A bag holds $2$ red counters, $2$ blue counters and $1$ white counter.

Two counters are taken at random.

Work out the probability that the two colours differ.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.

scheme.for: $\frac{2}{5} \times \frac{1}{4}$ for each of red-red and blue-blue (white-white cannot happen)

hints: With one white counter, white then white cannot happen.
Find the same colour, then take it from 1.
parts.workedSolution: Same colour: red-red $\tfrac{2}{20}$ and blue-blue $\tfrac{2}{20}$; white-white is impossible. So the same colour is $\tfrac{4}{20}$ and different colours is $1 - \tfrac{4}{20} = \tfrac{16}{20} = \tfrac{4}{5}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the same colour. Different colours is 1 minus it.
Each mixed pair can come in either order, so each counts twice.
Keeping 5 under the second pick puts the first counter back, and even lets white come twice.

parts.stem:
The probability that Maeve's bus is late is $0.15$.

If the bus is late, the probability that she misses registration is $0.8$.

If the bus is not late, the probability that she misses registration is $0.05$.

Complete the tree diagram.

rubric: After not late: misses 0.05, in time 0.95
Each pair of branches adds to 1

scheme.for: 0.85 on the not-late branch and the pair after a late bus, 0.8 and 0.2
The pair after a bus that is not late, 0.05 and 0.95

hints: Each 'if' sentence belongs to its own first branch.
Each pair of branches from one point adds to 1.
parts.workedSolution: Not late: $1 - 0.15 = 0.85$. After a late bus: misses $0.8$, in time $0.2$. After a bus that is not late: misses $0.05$, in time $0.95$.

parts.stem: Work out the probability that Maeve misses registration.
hints: Missing registration happens two ways.
Multiply along each branch, then add.

commonErrors.feedback: That is only the late-bus branch. She can also miss registration when the bus is on time, so that branch is added.
Those are the two 'if' chances on their own. Each is multiplied by its first branch before they are added.
The not-late branch carries 0.85, not 0.15.

emphasis: choosing from part of a group

context.setting: Roses and lilies at a garden centre, some in flower

parts.stem:
A garden centre has $180$ plants: $100$ roses and $80$ lilies.

The probability that a rose is in flower is $0.3$. The probability that a lily is in flower is $\tfrac{3}{4}$.

A plant that is in flower is chosen at random.

Work out the probability that it is a lily.

Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
hints: Turn each probability into a number of plants first.
The plant is chosen from those in flower.
parts.workedSolution: Roses in flower: $0.3 \times 100 = 30$. Lilies in flower: $\tfrac{3}{4} \times 80 = 60$. In flower: $90$. So $P(\text{lily}) = \tfrac{60}{90} = \tfrac{2}{3}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That divides by every plant. The plant is chosen from those in flower, so those go on the bottom.
That is the chance that a lily is in flower, not the chance that a flowering plant is a lily.
That is the chance that a plant is in flower. The question then chooses from those plants: how many of them are lilies?

findTheMistake.stem: Sean was asked: a bag holds $8$ mints and $5$ toffees, and two sweets are taken without replacement. Work out the probability that both are mints. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 uses the first-pick probability again, which is what happens when a sweet is put back. Without replacement the first mint stays out, so $8 - 1 = 7$ mints are left among $13 - 1 = 12$ sweets.
findTheMistake.feedback: Reading the words 'without replacement' and writing the second denominator down before anything else is what protects this mark. The method mark survives, because the structure of the working is right.

findTheMistake.stem: Aoife was asked: a box holds $4$ dark and $6$ milk chocolates, and two are taken without replacement. Work out the probability that both are dark. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 has both branch probabilities right and earns the method mark. Line 2 adds them. Along a branch both things have to happen, so the probabilities multiply; adding them here gives $11/15$, which is larger than $\tfrac{1}{2}$ even though taking two dark chocolates from a box that is mostly milk should be unlikely.
findTheMistake.feedback: A quick sense check catches this one: the answer should be well under a half, and it is not. Along a branch, multiply; across branches, add.

findTheMistake.stem: Niall was asked: a bag holds $3$ blue and $4$ white beads, and two are taken at random. Work out the probability that both beads match in colour. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: He added the tops, 3 + 2 = 5, but multiplied the bottoms. When fractions are multiplied, the tops multiply too: 3 × 2 = 6, so blue then blue is 6/42.
findTheMistake.feedback: The reports on the non-calculator paper keep finding this slip, not the method: multiply top by top and bottom by bottom, and cancel first where you can. The white product and the adding still earn their marks.

prompts.prompt: On a tree diagram, when do you multiply and when do you add?
prompts.answer: Multiply along a branch, because both events happen. Add across branches, because either one will do.

prompts.prompt: A bag holds $7$ blue and $5$ yellow counters. Two are taken without replacement. What is $P(\text{both blue})$?
Without replacement, what happens to the second pick's numerator and denominator?
prompts.answer: Denominator falls by one; numerator falls only if the same type was taken.

prompts.prompt: How do you find the probability of at least one?
prompts.answer: Work out the probability of none, and take it from 1.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for one of each colour. Why is one product not enough?
prompts.answer: Either colour can come first, so both orders count: add both products.

prompts.prompt: A probability answer comes out greater than 1. What has probably happened?
prompts.answer: Probabilities were added along a branch instead of multiplied; none can exceed 1.

prompts.prompt: How should a probability be written on the answer line?
prompts.answer: As a fraction, a decimal or a percentage, never as a ratio.

prompts.prompt: Why cancel before multiplying fractions on the non-calculator paper?
prompts.answer: The numbers stay small; the reports say marks go in fraction multiplication.

findings.asked: Non-replacement probabilities: show a given result, then a further probability.
findings.wentWrong: Most knew which products to form and over half added them correctly; fraction multiplication was the weakness.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Cancelled before multiplying and reached the further probability by subtracting the opposite event from 1.
findings.rule: Practise multiplying fractions by hand: the method marks depend on it.

findings.asked: Multiply three probabilities for a repeated event.
findings.wentWrong: Many added instead of multiplying, or could not multiply three simple fractions; some did two repetitions instead of three.

findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Wrote the second-pick fractions down before multiplying anything.

findings.wentWrong: A third got it; a third forgot the outcomes could occur in either order; a third had no idea what to do with the probabilities.
findings.rule: Both orders unless the question fixes the order.

findings.asked: A high-grade probability where pairs of numbers can be chosen in either order.
findings.wentWrong: Only the best recognised the suitable pairs and doubled for order.
findings.rule: Count the pairs, then count the orders.

findings.wentWrong: Majority full marks; losses came from poor fraction multiplication.

findings.rule: Tree, multiply along, add the matching branches.

findings.asked: A wordy probability: group sizes and a probability for each, then a choice from those who fit.
findings.wentWrong: About half worked it through; most of the rest started but could not carry the information to a conclusion.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Turned each probability into a number of people first, then divided by the group the choice was made from.
findings.rule: Count first, then choose from the right group.

findings.asked: Draw a tree for a biased dice rolled twice, then read a probability from it.
findings.wentWrong: Over 80 per cent drew a correct tree; the common error was leaving the labels off.
findings.rule: Every branch carries a label and a probability.

insight.ruleToRemember: Without replacement, denominators fall by one at each pick and numerators fall only when the same type was taken; multiply along each branch, add the branches that fit, include every order, and cancel before multiplying.
insight.aStarSignal: Non-calculator fraction products for three picks without replacement, with the orders counted and 'at least one' answered by subtracting the opposite event from 1.
